html:
States of matter carries about two questions in the paper (our estimate from the MEC topic list).

It is a wide chapter, so the questions spread: a gas-law or kinetic-theory calculation (combined gas equation, Graham's law, partial pressure, rms speed), a real-gas idea (van der Waals constants, when gases behave ideally), a liquid property (vapour pressure, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity, liquid crystals, solubility curves) or a solid-state fact (crystalline versus amorphous, deliquescent versus hygroscopic, crystal systems, atoms per unit cell).

Most are one-line answers if the relations are learnt as proportionalities.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Kinetic theory: average KE = (3/2)RT per mole, depends only on T; u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}; u_{mp} : u_{av} : u_{rms} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.
  • Gas laws: Boyle, Charles, pressure law, Avogadro → PV = nRT; combined P_1V_1/T_1 = P_2V_2/T_2 (T in kelvin); Dalton p_i = x_iP; Graham r \propto 1/\sqrt{M}.
  • Real gases: Z = PV/nRT; van der Waals a (attraction) and b (volume); ideal at low P and high T.
  • Liquids: vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and T; boiling point when VP = external pressure; surface tension and viscosity fall with temperature; liquid crystals are the mesophase.
  • Solids: crystalline (sharp mp, anisotropic) versus amorphous (softening range, isotropic); efflorescent, deliquescent, hygroscopic; water of crystallisation.
  • 7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais lattices; Z = 1, 2, 4 and coordination 6, 8, 12 for simple, body-centred and face-centred cubic; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A).

6.1 Gases: kinetic theory, gas laws, ideal and combined gas equations, deviation of real gases

Kinetic theory of gases

The postulates (for an ideal gas):

  1. A gas consists of a very large number of tiny particles whose own volume is negligible compared with the volume of the container.
  2. The particles move randomly in straight lines in all directions, colliding with one another and with the walls; the pressure is due to collisions with the walls.
  3. The collisions are perfectly elastic (no loss of total kinetic energy).
  4. There are no forces of attraction or repulsion between the particles.
  5. The average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature.

From these follows the kinetic gas equation, PV = \frac{1}{3}mNu_{rms}^2, and with PV = RT for one mole:

E_k = \frac{3}{2}RT \ \text{per mole}, \qquad \bar{\varepsilon} = \frac{3}{2}kT \ \text{per molecule}, \qquad u_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3P}{\rho}}

(k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹; M in kg mol⁻¹ when R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.) At a given temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy; lighter molecules simply move faster. At absolute zero the kinetic energy would be zero.

Speed Formula Relative value
Most probable, u_{mp} \sqrt{2RT/M} 1
Average (mean), u_{av} \sqrt{8RT/\pi M} 1.128
Root mean square, u_{rms} \sqrt{3RT/M} 1.224

The gas laws

Law Statement (fixed amount of gas) Form
Boyle (1662) at constant T, volume is inversely proportional to pressure PV = constant; P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
Charles (1787) at constant P, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature V/T = constant; V_t = V₀(1 + t/273)
Pressure law (Gay-Lussac) at constant V, pressure is directly proportional to absolute temperature P/T = constant
Avogadro at constant T and P, volume is proportional to the number of moles V/n = constant
Combined all of the above together P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂

Charles's law, extrapolated, gives zero volume at −273.15 °C — absolute zero, the origin of the kelvin scale (T/K = t/°C + 273).

Graph shapes are a favourite: P against V is a rectangular hyperbola; P against 1/V, and V against T, are straight lines through the origin; PV against P (at constant T) is a horizontal line.

The ideal gas equation

PV = nRT, \qquad n = \frac{w}{M} \;\Rightarrow\; PV = \frac{w}{M}RT, \qquad \rho = \frac{PM}{RT}

R in Value
J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ (SI) 8.314
L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ 0.0821
cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ 1.987 (≈ 2)

R is the work done by one mole of an ideal gas when it is heated through 1 K at constant pressure; it has the same value for all gases. An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT exactly at all temperatures and pressures; no real gas does.

Combined gas equation

Problem. A gas occupies 500 mL at 27 °C and 1.0 atm. Find its volume at 177 °C and 1.5 atm.

Solution. Convert to kelvin: 300 K and 450 K. V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 500 × (1.0/1.5) × (450/300) = 500 mL — the two changes cancel exactly. Never put °C into a gas law.

Dalton's law of partial pressures

The total pressure of a mixture of non-reacting gases equals the sum of their partial pressures (the pressure each would exert alone in the whole volume): P = p_1 + p_2 + \ldots, and p_i = x_iP where x_i is the mole fraction.

A gas collected over water is saturated with water vapour, so p(dry gas) = P(total) − aqueous tension (the vapour pressure of water at that temperature).

Graham's law of diffusion

At constant temperature and pressure, the rate of diffusion (or effusion) of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its density, and hence of its molar mass:

\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\rho_2}{\rho_1}} = \sqrt{\frac{M_2}{M_1}}, \qquad \text{and for equal volumes } \frac{t_1}{t_2} = \sqrt{\frac{M_1}{M_2}}

Uses: separating ²³⁵UF₆ from ²³⁸UF₆; finding molar masses.

When NH₃ and HCl are released at the two ends of a tube, NH₃ (M = 17) travels √(36.5/17) = 1.47 times faster than HCl, so the white ring of NH₄Cl forms nearer the HCl end (about 59 % of the way from the NH₃ end).

Graham's law in one line

Problem. A gas takes 3 times as long as oxygen to effuse through the same hole under the same conditions. Find its molar mass.

Solution. t ∝ √M, so M = 32 × 3² = 288 g mol⁻¹. (Squaring the time ratio is the step most often forgotten.)

Deviation of real gases from ideality

Real gases deviate because two postulates are false: the molecules do have volume and they do attract one another. The deviation is measured by the compressibility factor

Z = \frac{PV}{nRT}

Z = 1 for an ideal gas. Z < 1 (more compressible than ideal) when attractions dominate — moderate pressures, for easily liquefied gases such as CO₂ and NH₃.

Z > 1 when the molecular volume dominates — at high pressure for all gases, and at all pressures for H₂ and He at room temperature. Real gases behave most ideally at low pressure and high temperature.

The van der Waals equation corrects both postulates:

\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT

  • a measures the attractive forces (pressure correction, unit atm L² mol⁻²). Easily liquefied gases (NH₃, SO₂, CO₂) have large a; H₂ and He have very small a.
  • b is the excluded volume (volume correction, unit L mol⁻¹), about four times the actual volume of the molecules in one mole.
  • Boyle temperature T_B = a/Rb: the temperature at which a real gas obeys Boyle's law over a range of pressure. Critical temperature T_c = 8a/27Rb: above it a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone (CO₂ 31 °C, NH₃ 132 °C, O₂ −119 °C, He −268 °C).
Gas-law slips the options are built on

Celsius instead of kelvin; M in g mol⁻¹ with R = 8.314 J (it must be kg mol⁻¹ — the answer comes out √1000 ≈ 31.6 times too small); forgetting to square the time ratio in Graham's law; and using total moles instead of the mole fraction for a partial pressure.

6.2 Liquids: vapour pressure, boiling point, surface tension, viscosity, liquid crystals, solubility and solubility curves

Vapour pressure and boiling point

Evaporation is the escape of the fastest surface molecules at any temperature; it cools the liquid left behind.

In a closed vessel evaporation and condensation reach a dynamic equilibrium, and the pressure of the vapour then is the vapour pressure.

It depends only on the nature of the liquid and the temperature — not on the amount of liquid, the surface area or the volume of the vessel.

It rises steeply with temperature, and it is high for liquids with weak intermolecular forces (diethyl ether > ethanol > water at the same temperature).

Boiling point

A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure. The normal boiling point is the boiling temperature at 1 atm (760 mmHg): water 100 °C.

Lower the external pressure and the boiling point falls: water boils at about 95 °C in Kathmandu (about 1400 m, near 640 mmHg) and at about 70 °C on the summit of Mount Everest, so food cooks slowly there.

A pressure cooker raises the pressure, and so the boiling point, to about 120 °C. Water at 25 °C has a vapour pressure of 23.8 mmHg.

Surface tension

Surface tension

Surface tension is the force acting per unit length at right angles to an imaginary line drawn on the surface of a liquid. SI unit N m⁻¹ (also J m⁻², energy per unit area; CGS dyne cm⁻¹).

A molecule inside the liquid is pulled equally in all directions; one at the surface is pulled inwards only, so the surface behaves like a stretched skin and tends to minimise its area.

Results: drops and bubbles are spherical; water rises in a narrow glass capillary (mercury falls); insects walk on water; a needle floats.

Surface tension decreases as temperature rises (it vanishes at the critical temperature) and is lowered sharply by soaps and detergents. Water's value (about 72 mN m⁻¹ at 25 °C) is high because of hydrogen bonding.

With a stalagmometer (drop-number method), \gamma_1/\gamma_2 = \rho_1 n_2/(\rho_2 n_1) — fewer, bigger drops mean a higher surface tension.

Viscosity

Viscosity

Viscosity is the internal resistance of a fluid to flow. The coefficient of viscosity η is the tangential force per unit area needed to maintain unit velocity gradient between two layers: F = \eta A\,(dv/dx).

SI unit N s m⁻² = Pa s (= kg m⁻¹ s⁻¹); CGS unit the poise (1 P = 0.1 Pa s). Its reciprocal is fluidity.

The viscosity of a liquid decreases with rising temperature (molecules gain energy to overcome attractions) — but the viscosity of a gas increases with temperature.

Strong intermolecular forces and large molecules raise viscosity: glycerol (three OH groups, extensive hydrogen bonding) ≫ ethylene glycol > water > diethyl ether.

With an Ostwald viscometer, \eta_1/\eta_2 = \rho_1 t_1/(\rho_2 t_2).

Liquid crystals

Some organic substances with long, rod-like molecules melt first to a cloudy fluid that flows like a liquid but keeps some of the orientational order of a crystal — the liquid crystal (mesomorphic) state.

Reinitzer (1888) saw it in cholesteryl benzoate, which turns cloudy at 145 °C and clear at 179 °C.

Type Order Note
Nematic (thermotropic) molecules parallel, not in layers used in LCD screens
Smectic (thermotropic) parallel and arranged in layers most ordered
Cholesteric (thermotropic) layers twisted one over another colour changes with temperature
Lyotropic formed on dissolving in a solvent soap solutions, cell membranes

Uses: liquid crystal displays (watches, calculators, phones, televisions), temperature strips and thermometers, and medical thermography (locating tumours and blocked blood vessels by skin temperature).

Solubility and solubility curves

Solubility is the mass of solute (in grams) that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to give a saturated solution at a stated temperature. A solubility curve plots it against temperature.

  • Most solids dissolve better when hot; KNO₃, NH₄Cl and KCl strongly, NaCl only slightly. A few become less soluble on heating — Ca(OH)₂, Li₂SO₄ and Ce₂(SO₄)₃.
  • A kink marks a change of the solid phase (Na₂SO₄·10H₂O → Na₂SO₄ at 32.4 °C).
  • Gases become less soluble as temperature rises and more soluble as pressure rises (Henry's law) — that is why fish need cool, oxygen-rich water and why a soft drink fizzes when opened.
  • Uses of curves: finding the mass that crystallises on cooling (difference of two solubilities), choosing a method of crystallisation (cooling for KNO₃, evaporation for NaCl), and separating salts by fractional crystallisation.
Mass crystallising on cooling

Problem. A solution of KNO₃ saturated at 60 °C contains 100 g of water. How much KNO₃ crystallises when it is cooled to 20 °C? (Solubility 110 g and 31.6 g per 100 g water.)

Solution. Mass that crystallises = 110 − 31.6 = 78.4 g. (For w grams of water, scale by w/100.) The same cooling would deposit only about 1.2 g of NaCl from its saturated solution, which is why salt is crystallised by evaporation instead.

6.3 Solids: crystalline and amorphous solids; efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic substances; water of crystallisation

Crystalline and amorphous solids

Property Crystalline Amorphous
Arrangement of particles regular, repeating, long-range order irregular, only short-range order
Shape definite geometric shape no definite shape
Melting sharp melting point soften over a range of temperature
Heat of fusion definite not definite
Physical properties with direction anisotropic (differ with direction) isotropic (same in all directions)
Cutting clean cleavage along planes irregular fracture
Nature true solids pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids
Examples NaCl, quartz, diamond, sugar, ice, metals glass, rubber, plastics, fused silica, pitch

Quartz (crystalline SiO₂) and fused silica glass (amorphous SiO₂) are the same compound in the two forms. Amorphous solids are often called pseudo-solids or supercooled liquids: their particles are frozen in the disorder of a liquid.

Efflorescent, deliquescent and hygroscopic substances

Term Behaviour in moist air Examples
Efflorescent loses water of crystallisation to the air and crumbles to a powder washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O, Glauber's salt Na₂SO₄·10H₂O, FeSO₄·7H₂O
Deliquescent absorbs so much moisture that it dissolves in it CaCl₂, NaOH, KOH, MgCl₂, FeCl₃, ZnCl₂
Hygroscopic absorbs moisture but does not dissolve (or is a liquid that takes up water) quicklime CaO, silica gel, anhydrous CuSO₄, P₄O₁₀, conc. H₂SO₄

A hydrate effloresces when its own water-vapour pressure is greater than the partial pressure of water in the air; a solid deliquesces when its saturated solution has a vapour pressure lower than that of the air.

Deliquescent and hygroscopic substances are drying agents: fused CaCl₂, quicklime (for ammonia), conc. H₂SO₄, P₄O₁₀ and silica gel.

Common salt becomes damp in the rainy season only because of traces of deliquescent MgCl₂ and CaCl₂ in it.

Deliquescent is not the same as hygroscopic

Both absorb water. A deliquescent solid ends up as a solution; a hygroscopic solid only becomes damp. Every deliquescent substance is hygroscopic, but not every hygroscopic substance is deliquescent.

Crystallisation and water of crystallisation

Crystallisation purifies a solid: dissolve it in the minimum of hot solvent, filter hot, and cool slowly; crystals separate and soluble impurities stay in the mother liquor.

A crystal grows by nucleation (a tiny ordered cluster forms) followed by growth (more particles add to its faces); slow, undisturbed cooling gives fewer, larger crystals.

Water of crystallisation

The water of crystallisation is the fixed number of water molecules combined with one formula unit of a salt in its crystals. It is responsible for the shape (and often the colour) of the crystals and is driven off on heating: CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue) → CuSO₄ (white)

  • 5H₂O.
Name Formula Name Formula
Blue vitriol CuSO₄·5H₂O Washing soda Na₂CO₃·10H₂O
Green vitriol FeSO₄·7H₂O Glauber's salt Na₂SO₄·10H₂O
White vitriol ZnSO₄·7H₂O Gypsum CaSO₄·2H₂O
Epsom salt MgSO₄·7H₂O Plaster of Paris CaSO₄·½H₂O
Borax Na₂B₄O₇·10H₂O Potash alum K₂SO₄·Al₂(SO₄)₃·24H₂O
Mohr's salt FeSO₄·(NH₄)₂SO₄·6H₂O Hypo Na₂S₂O₃·5H₂O
Finding x in a hydrate

Problem. Crystals of Na₂CO₃·xH₂O lose 62.9 % of their mass when heated to constant mass. Find x. (Na₂CO₃ = 106)

Solution. 18x/(106 + 18x) = 0.629 → 18x(1 − 0.629) = 66.7 → x = 66.7/6.68 = 10 (washing soda).

6.4 The unit cell, the seven crystal systems and the fourteen Bravais lattices; types of crystalline solid by bonding

Lattice, unit cell and crystal systems

Crystal lattice and unit cell

A crystal lattice (space lattice) is the regular three-dimensional array of points that shows the positions of the particles in a crystal.

The unit cell is the smallest portion of the lattice which, repeated in three dimensions, generates the whole crystal. It is described by the edge lengths a, b, c and the angles α, β, γ between them.

Only seven crystal systems are possible, and placing particles at corners, body centres, face centres or end-face centres gives fourteen Bravais lattices in all (Bravais, 1848).

Crystal system Edges Angles Bravais lattices Examples
Cubic a = b = c α = β = γ = 90° 3 (simple, body-centred, face-centred) NaCl, Cu, diamond, ZnS
Tetragonal a = b ≠ c α = β = γ = 90° 2 (simple, body-centred) white tin, SnO₂, TiO₂
Orthorhombic a ≠ b ≠ c α = β = γ = 90° 4 (simple, body, face, end-centred) rhombic sulphur, KNO₃, BaSO₄
Monoclinic a ≠ b ≠ c α = γ = 90°, β ≠ 90° 2 (simple, end-centred) monoclinic sulphur, Na₂SO₄·10H₂O
Triclinic a ≠ b ≠ c α ≠ β ≠ γ ≠ 90° 1 CuSO₄·5H₂O, K₂Cr₂O₇, H₃BO₃
Hexagonal a = b ≠ c α = β = 90°, γ = 120° 1 graphite, ZnO, Mg, ice
Rhombohedral (trigonal) a = b = c α = β = γ ≠ 90° 1 calcite (CaCO₃), cinnabar (HgS), NaNO₃

3 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 14. The cubic system is the most symmetrical and the triclinic the least.

Counting particles in cubic unit cells

A corner particle is shared by 8 unit cells (contributes 1/8), an edge particle by 4 (1/4), a face-centre particle by 2 (1/2), and a body-centre particle belongs wholly to its cell.

Cubic cell Atoms per cell, Z Coordination number Edge and radius Packing efficiency
Simple (primitive) 1 6 a = 2r 52.4 %
Body-centred (bcc) 2 8 √3 a = 4r 68 %
Face-centred (fcc, ccp) 4 12 √2 a = 4r 74 %

The density of a cubic crystal follows from the unit cell:

\rho = \frac{Z \times M}{a^3 \times N_A}

(a in cm gives ρ in g cm⁻³.) Examples: Na, K and Fe (at room temperature) are bcc; Cu, Ag, Au and Al are fcc; NaCl has 4 formula units per cubic cell.

Density of rock salt

Problem. NaCl has a face-centred cubic cell with edge 564 pm and 4 formula units per cell. Find its density (NaCl = 58.5 g mol⁻¹, N_A = 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹).

Solution. a = 5.64 × 10⁻⁸ cm, a³ = 1.794 × 10⁻²² cm³. ρ = \dfrac{4 \times 58.5}{1.794 \times 10⁻^{2}^{2} \times 6.02 \times 10^{2}^{3}} = 234/108 = 2.17 g cm⁻³ — the measured value, which confirms the structure.

Types of crystalline solid by bonding

Type Particles Forces Properties Examples
Ionic cations and anions electrostatic (ionic) bonds hard, brittle, high mp; conduct only when molten or dissolved NaCl, KNO₃, MgO, CaF₂
Covalent (network) atoms covalent bonds throughout very hard, very high mp, non-conductors (graphite excepted) diamond, quartz SiO₂, SiC, graphite
Molecular molecules van der Waals forces or hydrogen bonds soft, low mp, often volatile, insulators I₂, dry ice (CO₂), naphthalene, ice, S₈, P₄
Metallic positive kernels in an electron sea metallic bonds lustrous, malleable, ductile, good conductors; mp varies Na, Cu, Fe, Ag

Graphite is the classic exception: a covalent solid that conducts, because each carbon (sp²) leaves one electron delocalised over its layer; the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces, so it is soft and slippery.

Formula and fact sheet

Quantity Formula
Kinetic gas equation PV = \frac{1}{3}mNu_{rms}^2
Kinetic energy (3/2)RT per mole; (3/2)kT per molecule; depends only on T
Molecular speeds u_{mp} = \sqrt{2RT/M}, u_{av} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}, u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}; u_{mp} : u_{av} : u_{rms} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224
Gas laws PV = const (T); V/T = const (P); P/T = const (V); V/n = const
Ideal and combined PV = nRT; ρ = PM/RT; P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂
R 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ = 1.987 cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹
Dalton P = Σpᵢ; pᵢ = xᵢP; p(dry) = P − aqueous tension
Graham r₁/r₂ = √(M₂/M₁) = √(ρ₂/ρ₁); t₁/t₂ = √(M₁/M₂)
Real gases Z = PV/nRT; (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT; T_B = a/Rb; T_c = 8a/27Rb
Surface tension (drops) γ₁/γ₂ = ρ₁n₂/(ρ₂n₁); unit N m⁻¹
Viscosity (Ostwald) η₁/η₂ = ρ₁t₁/(ρ₂t₂); unit Pa s; 1 P = 0.1 Pa s
Unit cell Z = 1, 2, 4 (sc, bcc, fcc); CN 6, 8, 12; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A)

Facts: 7 crystal systems and 14 Bravais lattices; liquid viscosity and surface tension fall with temperature (gas viscosity rises); boiling point is where VP = external pressure (water: about 95 °C in Kathmandu, about 70 °C on Everest); efflorescent loses water, deliquescent dissolves in absorbed water, hygroscopic merely absorbs it.

Chapter summary

  • Kinetic theory: random elastic motion, no attractions, negligible molecular volume; KE = (3/2)RT per mole for every gas; u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} and u_{mp} : u_{av} : u_{rms} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.
  • Boyle, Charles, pressure and Avogadro laws combine into PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J or 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); always use kelvin.
  • Dalton: p_i = x_iP; Graham: rate ∝ 1/√M (lighter gases diffuse faster; time ∝ √M).
  • Real gases: Z = PV/nRT; van der Waals a (attraction) and b (excluded volume); ideal behaviour at low P and high T; large a means easy liquefaction.
  • Vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and T; boiling occurs when VP = external pressure. Surface tension (N m⁻¹) and liquid viscosity (Pa s) fall as T rises.
  • Liquid crystals (nematic, smectic, cholesteric) flow but keep orientational order; used in LCDs and thermometers. Solubility curves show crystallisation yields; KNO₃ rises steeply, NaCl barely.
  • Crystalline solids: long-range order, sharp mp, anisotropic; amorphous: short-range order, soften over a range, isotropic. Efflorescent loses water; deliquescent dissolves; hygroscopic absorbs.
  • 7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais lattices; sc, bcc, fcc have Z = 1, 2, 4 and CN 6, 8, 12; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A). Solids are ionic, covalent network, molecular or metallic.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (c) — KE = (3/2)RT per mole: it depends on the absolute temperature only, not on P, V or the kind of gas.

2. (a) — P ∝ 1/V at constant T, so PV is constant. V/T = constant is Charles's law; P/T = constant the pressure law.

3. (b) — 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. 8.314 is in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ and 1.987 in cal mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; 22.4 L is the molar volume.

4. (d) — r ∝ 1/√ρ ∝ 1/√M. Option (b) misses the square root.

5. (a) — At low pressure the molecular volume is negligible, and at high temperature the attractions hardly matter.

6. (c) — a corrects the pressure for intermolecular attraction; b corrects the volume for the size of the molecules.

7. (d) — Boiling begins when bubbles of vapour can form inside the liquid, i.e. when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it.

8. (b) — Force per unit length: N m⁻¹ (equivalently J m⁻²). N s m⁻² is the unit of viscosity.

9. (a) — Warmer molecules overcome intermolecular attraction more easily, so the liquid flows more freely. (Gas viscosity does the opposite.)

10. (c) — Deliquescent solids, such as CaCl₂ and NaOH, dissolve in the water they absorb; hygroscopic ones only become damp.

11. (b) — Glass has only short-range order and softens over a range of temperature. NaCl, quartz and diamond are crystalline.

12. (d) — Seven crystal systems give fourteen Bravais lattices.

13. (c) — The liquid crystal (mesophase) lies between the crystalline solid and the isotropic liquid.

14. (a) — 8 corners × 1/8 + 6 face centres × 1/2 = 1 + 3 = 4.

  1. State the gas laws, derive the ideal gas equation and explain Graham's law, Dalton's law and deviations of real gases with numericals. [10]

Model answer D1: gas laws, ideal gas equation and real gases (10 marks)

Introduction. A gas has no fixed shape or volume, and its state is given by pressure P, volume V, temperature T and amount n.

Gas laws.

Law Statement Expression
Boyle V \propto 1/P at constant T P_1V_1 = P_2V_2
Charles V \propto T at constant P V_1/T_1 = V_2/T_2
Gay-Lussac P \propto T at constant V P_1/T_1 = P_2/T_2
Avogadro V \propto n at constant T and P V/n constant

Ideal gas equation. Combining the laws gives PV = nRT, where R = 0.0821\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} = 8.314\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}. Also PM = dRT, so the density of a gas is d = PM/RT.

Dalton's law of partial pressures. P_{total} = p_1 + p_2 + \cdots and p_i = x_iP_{total}.

Graham's law of diffusion. At constant T and P, the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the density (or molar mass): \dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{M_2}{M_1}}.

Kinetic theory results. PV = \tfrac13mN\overline{c^2}; the average kinetic energy is \tfrac32kT; u_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M}, the most probable speed \sqrt{2RT/M} and the average speed \sqrt{8RT/\pi M}, in the ratio 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.

Real gases. At high pressure and low temperature, gases deviate from ideal behaviour, because the molecular volume is not negligible and the attractions are not zero.

The van der Waals equation is \left(P + \dfrac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT, where a corrects for attraction and b for volume. The compressibility factor is Z = PV/nRT (Z = 1 for an ideal gas).

Above the critical temperature a gas cannot be liquefied by pressure alone. The Boyle temperature is T_B = a/Rb.

Numerical.

  • 2\ \text{g} of H₂ (1\ \text{mol}) at 27^{\circ}\text{C} in 10\ \text{L}: P = \dfrac{1\times0.0821\times300}{10} = 2.46\ \text{atm}.
  • Graham: \dfrac{r_{H_2}}{r_{O_2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{32}{2}} = 4, so hydrogen diffuses four times as fast as oxygen.
  • Density of CO₂ at STP = \dfrac{1\times44}{0.0821\times273} = 1.96\ \text{g L}^{-1}.
  • u_{rms} of O₂ at 300\ \text{K} = \sqrt{\dfrac{3\times8.314\times300}{0.032}} = 484\ \text{m s}^{-1}.

Conclusion. PV = nRT describes an ideal gas, and the van der Waals equation corrects it for molecular size and attractions.

Model answer D2: liquids and crystalline solids (10 marks)

Introduction. Liquids have definite volume but no definite shape, while crystalline solids have a regular, long-range arrangement of particles.

Properties of liquids.

  1. Vapour pressure: the pressure of the vapour in equilibrium with the liquid. It rises with temperature, and the liquid boils when it equals the external pressure. The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is \log\dfrac{p_2}{p_1} = \dfrac{\Delta H_{vap}}{2.303R}\left(\dfrac1{T_1} - \dfrac1{T_2}\right).
  2. Surface tension: the force per unit length acting along the surface, which causes spherical drops and capillary rise. It decreases as the temperature rises.
  3. Viscosity: resistance to flow, which decreases as the temperature rises for liquids.
  4. Hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point of water (100^{\circ}\text{C}) above that of H₂S.

Crystal lattices. The unit cell is the smallest repeating unit. The three cubic types:

Unit cell Atoms per cell Z Coordination number Packing efficiency Relation of a and r
Simple cubic 1 6 52.4\% a = 2r
Body-centred cubic 2 8 68\% \sqrt3a = 4r
Face-centred cubic (ccp) 4 12 74\% \sqrt2a = 4r

Hexagonal close packing also has 74\% and coordination number 12. In a close-packed structure of N atoms there are N octahedral voids and 2N tetrahedral voids.

Density of a unit cell. \rho = \dfrac{ZM}{N_Aa^3}.

Types of solid. Ionic (NaCl), covalent network (diamond, SiC), molecular (ice, I₂) and metallic (Cu). Defects: Schottky (missing ion pairs, density decreases, in NaCl) and Frenkel (an ion shifts to an interstitial site, density unchanged, in AgCl).

Numerical. NaCl is fcc with Z = 4, M = 58.5\ \text{g mol}^{-1} and a = 564\ \text{pm}: \rho = \dfrac{4\times58.5}{6.022\times10^{23}\times(5.64\times10^{-8})^3} = 2.17\ \text{g cm}^{-3}.

For copper (fcc) with a = 361\ \text{pm}, r = \dfrac{\sqrt2\times361}{4} = 127.6\ \text{pm}.

Conclusion. fcc and hcp are the most efficient packings (74\%), and the density of a crystal follows from \rho = ZM/N_Aa^3.
